title: API & Event Compatibility: Versioning and Schema Evolution
summary: Quick revision notes on keeping APIs and event streams compatible as they change: compatibility directions, URI vs header versioning, Avro/Protobuf schema evolution with a schema registry, deprecation, tolerant readers and expand-and-contract migrations.

chapters.title: Compatibility Fundamentals and Mental Model
points: Backward compatible: new consumer/code can read data or calls produced by the OLD version; forward compatible: old consumer can read data produced by the NEW version
Breaking change = anything that makes a working client fail: removing or renaming a field, changing a type, making an optional field required, changing semantics or error codes
Safe (non-breaking) changes: adding an optional field, adding a new endpoint, adding an enum value only if consumers tolerate unknowns
Full compatibility = both directions at once; needed when producers and consumers deploy independently and you cannot control rollout order
Same field name with changed meaning (e.g. amount cents to dollars) is the worst break: it passes every schema check but corrupts data silently

chapters.title: API Versioning: URI vs Header
points: URI versioning: /v1/orders, /v2/orders; visible, cacheable, easy to route and test with curl, but version is not part of the resource identity and URLs proliferate
Header versioning: Accept: application/vnd.acme.v2+json (media type) or custom header X-API-Version: 2; clean URLs, but hidden, harder to test in a browser and caches must Vary on that header
Query param versioning (?version=2) is simple but easy to omit; always define a default version when the client sends none
Version only on breaking changes, not every release; prefer additive changes so most clients never move versions
Pick one scheme per API and apply it consistently; running v1 and v2 side by side doubles maintenance, so cap supported versions (e.g. N and N-1)

chapters.title: Schema Evolution for Events: Avro, Protobuf, Registry
points: Schema registry stores versioned schemas per subject (e.g. orders-value); messages carry only a schema ID, and the registry rejects a new schema that violates the subject's compatibility mode

Registry modes: BACKWARD (default; new schema reads old data, so upgrade consumers first), FORWARD (old reads new, upgrade producers first), FULL, and the _TRANSITIVE variants that check against all versions, not just the latest
Avro: reader and writer schemas are resolved at read time; added fields need a default to stay backward compatible, only fields with defaults may be removed, and renames need aliases

Protobuf: identity is the field number, never the name; never reuse or renumber a field, mark removed ones with reserved 4; reserved "old_name", and new fields default to zero values so absence is ambiguous
Protobuf has no required in proto3 and unknown fields are preserved/ignored; Avro has no field numbers, so it depends on the schema being present at read time (hence the registry)

chapters.title: Deprecation, Tolerant Reader and Expand-Contract
points: Tolerant reader (Postel): consumer ignores unknown fields, reads only what it needs, and does not fail on new enum values or extra JSON properties; the main enabler of forward compatibility

Deprecation workflow: announce, mark in docs/OpenAPI (deprecated: true), emit Deprecation and Sunset headers (RFC 9745 Deprecation: @<unix-seconds>; Sunset: HTTP date), monitor per-client usage, then remove only after usage hits zero
Expand and contract (parallel change) for a breaking change: 1 expand (add new field/column/endpoint, keep old), 2 migrate (dual-write, move readers one by one), 3 contract (remove old once unused)
Renaming a field via expand-contract: add new_name, write both, switch readers, stop writing old_name, then delete it, each step an independently deployable release
Contract tests (e.g. Pact) and schema-diff checks in CI (buf breaking, registry compatibility API) catch breaks before merge

chapters.title: Compatibility Cheat Sheet
points: Safe: add optional field or endpoint. Breaking: remove/rename field, change type or meaning, add required field, reuse a Protobuf number
Registry: BACKWARD means upgrade consumers first; FORWARD means upgrade producers first; FULL or TRANSITIVE when rollout order is unknown
URI /v2 = visible and cacheable; header Accept vnd.v2 = clean URLs but add Vary; always default the version
Deprecate: announce, Deprecation + Sunset headers, track usage, remove at zero
Break safely: expand (add new, keep old), migrate (dual-write, move readers), contract (remove old); consumers must be tolerant readers
